issues.legal_issue: Owners who did not object to an acquisition notification cannot rely on its quashing in other owners’ cases to invalidate the acquisition as against their own land.
material_facts: The landowners did not file objections to the acquisition notification.
A prior judgment had allowed other landowners’ petitions on grounds relating to the inquiry into objections and quashed the later acquisition declaration in those cases.
The landowners relied on that prior judgment, and the High Court treated it as invalidating the declaration for all affected owners.
issues.conclusion: The landowners could not claim the benefit of the quashing in other owners’ cases. Because they had filed no objections, the declaration remained in force as against them, and the earlier quashing did not cause the initial notification to lapse for their land.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1), 5A and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, persons who filed no objections to the Section 4(1) notification could not challenge the Section 5A inquiry or obtain the benefit of its alleged defects. The Court applied the three-Judge decision in Abhey Ram v. Union of India, which held that such owners could not rely on the quashing of the Section 6 declaration in other owners’ cases; it preferred that decision to the two-Judge decision in Delhi Development Authority v. Sudan Singh.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_judgment: The matter is an appeal from a judgment allowing a writ petition concerning an acquisition.
predicates.owners_filed_no_objections: The owners did not submit objections to the notification concerning their land.
predicates.prior_quashing_arose_from_other_owners_c: The earlier quashing followed challenges brought by other owners, rather than by the owners seeking to rely on it.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a writ judgment concerns owners who filed no objections and the earlier quashing arose from other owners’ cases, those owners cannot rely on that quashing.

issues.legal_issue: Quashing an acquisition declaration in individual owners’ cases does not, without more, quash the declaration for all owners covered by it.
material_facts: A prior Division Bench had allowed petitions brought by some owners and quashed the acquisition declaration in those cases.
The present landowners had not filed objections and were not among the petitioners in those earlier cases.
The High Court treated the earlier judgment as a judgment applying to all owners, while the three-Judge decision in Abhey Ram had interpreted its effect as limited to the cases before that court.
issues.conclusion: The earlier Division Bench judgment did not quash the entire declaration for all owners. The Court was bound by the three-Judge decision in Abhey Ram, which had interpreted the earlier judgment as case-specific.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed the three-Judge decision in Abhey Ram v. Union of India, which considered the effect of the earlier Division Bench judgment and held that quashing in individual writ petitions did not quash the whole declaration. That larger-Bench decision governed over the two-Judge decision in Delhi Development Authority v. Sudan Singh; dismissal of a special leave petition and non-binding departmental legal opinions could not override it.

predicates.appeal_concerns_same_acquisition: The appeal concerns the same acquisition as the one involved in the earlier judgment.
predicates.earlier_quashing_followed_individual_pet: The earlier declaration was quashed in proceedings brought by individual owners.
predicates.larger_bench_interpreted_earlier_judgmen: A larger judicial bench interpreted the earlier judgment as applying to the individual cases before it rather than to all affected owners.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns the same acquisition, an earlier quashing followed individual petitions, and a larger bench interpreted that judgment as case-specific, the earlier quashing was not universal.

issues.legal_issue: The reasoning that individual stay orders suspended further steps for an integrated acquisition does not make a later quashing in individual cases apply to the entire acquisition declaration.
material_facts: The acquisition was part of an integrated scheme.
The earlier Full Bench considered whether the declaration had been issued outside the applicable time limit and held that individual stay orders prevented further steps on the integrated declaration.
The landowners argued that the same reasoning meant the later quashing in individual petitions must apply to the entire declaration.
issues.conclusion: The stay-order reasoning was confined to the time-limit issue and did not establish that quashing in individual cases invalidated the declaration for everyone.
issues.legal_principle: The Full Bench’s reasoning in Balak Ram Gupta v. Union of India concerned the effect of stay orders on the timing of a declaration for an integrated scheme. It did not determine the effect of later quashing in individual petitions. The Court applied Abhey Ram v. Union of India in holding that case-specific quashing was not quashing of the whole declaration.

predicates.challenge_concerns_time_limit_for_acquis: The issue under consideration is whether an acquisition declaration was made outside the applicable time limit.
predicates.acquisition_was_an_integrated_scheme: The acquisition formed part of a scheme treated as an integrated whole.
predicates.individual_stays_prevented_further_steps: Stay orders in individual proceedings prevented the authorities from taking further steps on the declaration.

issues.definition: When a time-limit challenge concerns an integrated acquisition and individual stays prevented further steps, the stay-order reasoning does not make later quashing in individual cases universal.
